description: A one-chord jazz-funk groove from Fat Albert Rotunda (1969), Hancock's Warner Bros. debut written for Bill Cosby's Fat Albert TV special. Buster Williams' bass and Joe Henderson's rare flute carry the slow build.

pops.text: Cartoon music, grown up: Hancock wrote this music for Hey, Hey, Hey, It's Fat Albert, Bill Cosby's 1969 NBC TV special — which later inspired Fat Albert and the Cosby Kids.
This was Hancock's Warner Bros. debut and his eighth album as a leader, arriving in December 1969 right after he left Blue Note Records.
He had just finished a five-year stint in Miles Davis's quintet. The playful R&B-funk here is a sharp left turn from that post-bop world.
Singer Gretchen Parlato's favorite detail: the whole track grooves on essentially one chord. Layered horns and repeated figures do all the moving.
That low end is Buster Williams on bass, building the track as a slow crescendo under Hancock's piano and the horns.
Hear that flute? It's tenor sax great Joe Henderson — on this session he played mostly flutes, a rare sound from him.
Recorded at Rudy Van Gelder's studio in Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey — the room behind countless classic jazz albums — with Van Gelder himself engineering.
Hancock produced and arranged it himself, playing piano and Fender Rhodes electric piano. The Rhodes glow became a signature of his next decade.
Vinyl trivia: 'Fat Mama' was the B-side of the 'Wiggle Waggle' single (Warner Bros. 7358). The A-side got the glory; this side got the groove.
Hip-hop afterlife: 2Pac sampled 'Fat Mama' on 'If My Homie Calls' from his 1991 debut 2Pacalypse Now. The cartoon groove became a rap foundation.

title: Fat Mama

description: Imagine Dragons' breakthrough: an electronic-rock sleeper hit from Night Visions (2012) that climbed for months, spent a then-record 87 weeks on the Hot 100, won a Grammy, and went Diamond in the US.

pops.text: Sleeper hit supreme: first sent to modern rock radio on October 29, 2012, it didn't reach pop radio until April 2013 — and just kept climbing.
Dan Reynolds calls it a song about an awakening: waking up one day and deciding to see life in a fresh way. The ash and dust are metaphorical.
Producer Alex da Kid co-wrote it. It's one of the darkest, most electronic tracks on Night Visions, with a real dubstep undertow.
The video, directed by Syndrome, skips the apocalypse for an underground puppet-fighting ring — starring Alexandra Daddario and Lou Diamond Phillips.
The hero is a pink teddy bear. It knocks out the champion puppet Gorigula with one punch, then zaps the bodyguards with laser vision. Naturally.
Chart tortoise: it broke the record for the slowest climb to the Hot 100 top 5, finally peaking at No. 3 — the band's first top 10 single.
It held the Hot 100 longevity record at 87 weeks for over seven years, and still holds the mark for most consecutive weeks, at 85.
At the 2014 Grammys it won Best Rock Performance. On the broadcast, the band debuted a remix with Kendrick Lamar, later released as a single.
Certified Diamond at 17x Platinum in the US, it's one of the best-selling singles ever — and was the third best-selling song in America in 2013.
Cover royalty: 'Weird Al' Yankovic parodied it as 'Inactive' in 2014, and Lindsey Stirling and Pentatonix's cover won a 2013 YouTube Award.

title: Radioactive

description: A rapid-fire arena anthem from Evolve (2017), produced by Joel Little. It topped Billboard's Hot Rock and Rock Airplay charts, peaked at No. 12 on the Hot 100, and its flooding-room video won an MTV VMA.

pops.text: It arrived May 9, 2017 as a promotional single, announced the same day the band revealed the title and artwork for Evolve on Twitter.
Producer is Joel Little, the New Zealander behind Lorde's early hits. He also shares a songwriting credit with all four band members.
The Guardian heard it as a song 'written with a sports highlights package in mind' — all adrenaline-in-my-veins verses and obligatory woah-oh choruses.
Sports got the memo: it was the official theme for WWE's Battleground pay-per-view and landed in the video game Madden NFL 18.
The video opens with Reynolds swimming through a flooded room. Spot the matchbooks: 'The Overlook Hotel' is a sly nod to The Shining.
Directors Matt Eastin and Aaron Hymes flood the room, add two sirens tugging at Reynolds, then — for the final chorus — set the whole stage on fire instead.
The clip won the MTV Video Music Award for Best Rock Video, and in February 2025 it passed one billion views on YouTube.
Chart run: No. 1 on both Hot Rock Songs and Rock Airplay, No. 1 on Adult Pop Airplay, and a No. 12 peak on the Hot 100 in May 2018 — a full year after release.
Hometown moment: on May 30, 2018 the band played it live before Game 2 of the Stanley Cup Final at T-Mobile Arena in their native Las Vegas.
In February 2018 the band publicly asked the Conservative Political Action Conference to stop using the song on its conference website.

title: Whatever It Takes

description: Johnson's gentlest protest song: a sunny-sounding critique of violent, sensational TV from In Between Dreams (2005). It topped Billboard's Adult Alternative chart and was certified Gold in the US.

pops.text: Don't let the sunshine fool you — Wikipedia classifies this one plainly: it's a protest song, aimed at contemporary television and its diet of violence.
The question in the chorus — where did all the good people go? — is about channel-surfing: Johnson says he's been changing channels and doesn't see them on the TV shows.
It's track 4 on In Between Dreams, Johnson's third album, released March 1, 2005 and recorded the previous October in Hawaii.
Recording home base: The Mango Tree studio in Hawaii. The album cover even pictures a mango tree in its honor.
That piano is Zach Gill, Johnson's longtime collaborator, who plays piano on this track and on 'Sitting, Waiting, Wishing.'
Producer Mario Caldato Jr. — a Beastie Boys collaborator — produced both this album and Johnson's previous one, On and On.
Released as a single on May 9, 2005, it followed 'Sitting, Waiting, Wishing' in the album's singles run, ahead of 'Breakdown.'
Chart peak: No. 1 on Billboard's Adult Alternative Songs chart, and No. 2 on Billboard's year-end Triple-A chart for 2005.
Abroad it was a modest hit: No. 25 in New Zealand, No. 50 in the UK and No. 92 in the Netherlands. The single was certified Gold in the US.
Johnson had visited this theme before: 'Cookie Jar' on On and On also questions media violence — but 'Good People' makes the protest sunnier and more explicit.

title: Good People

description: A 2:54 travel reverie from On and On (2003), Johnson's second album. Written from a teenage surf trip to Port Blair, it longs for when stars were just holes to heaven and there were fewer questions.

pops.text: Johnson has said he wrote this on an early surf trip with friends — and recalls it as the first song he wrote that made him think it could be a hit.
It's written from his teenage perspective: a time when friendship, surfing and the next adventure were enough, before life got complicated.
The place in the lyric is real: Port Blair, where the travelers get stuck 'where boats break and children stare,' is the capital of India's Andaman Islands.
Travel-diary details fill the verses: a seven-hour drive at dawn, square cars spitting diesel, and barefoot kids playing cricket.
It's track 8 on On and On, Johnson's second studio album, released May 6, 2003 — and at 2:54 it's a postcard, not an epic.
Just a trio on the record: Johnson on vocals and guitar, Adam Topol on drums and percussion, and Merlo Podlewski on bass.
Recorded in 2002 at The Mango Tree, Johnson's studio in Hawaii — the same room that hosted most of his early albums.
Producer was Mario Caldato Jr., best known for his work with the Beastie Boys. He also produced Johnson's next album, In Between Dreams.
The parent album was no sleeper: On and On peaked at No. 3 on the Billboard 200 and No. 1 in New Zealand, and went Platinum in the US.
The title image is pure kid astronomy: fewer questions back 'when stars were still just the holes to heaven.'

title: Holes To Heaven

description: A mostly instrumental power-trio jam from James Gang Rides Again, built around Joe Walsh's snarling riff. It only reached No. 59, then refused to leave classic-rock radio.

pops.text: Cleveland power trio alert: by this album the James Gang was just Joe Walsh, bassist Dale Peters and drummer Jim Fox — three people making a lot of noise.
Yes, there was a 'Funk #48' first — it appeared on the band's 1969 debut, Yer' Album. This is the sequel nobody numbered carefully.
Walsh's naming story: the band thought they'd played the jam about 50 times. Engineer Bill Szymczyk said it couldn't have been 50 — so, 'OK, 49 then!'
Szymczyk wasn't just engineer here — he produced James Gang Rides Again and later produced some of the Eagles' biggest records.
Spot the singing shortage: the album version runs 3:54 with only two verses. Most of the song is a vehicle for Walsh's guitar.
The lyrics are about a wild girlfriend the singer cannot tame. The guitar, frankly, sounds equally untamable.
Chart reality check: 'Funk #49' peaked at No. 59 on the Billboard Hot 100. Its classic-rock afterlife massively out-charted its chart life.
The parent album did better — James Gang Rides Again peaked at No. 20 on the Billboard 200 and went gold.
Pete Townshend was an early fan: impressed by Walsh, he invited the James Gang to tour Europe with The Who.
The count finally continued in 2012, when Walsh recorded 'Funk #50' for his solo album Analog Man. Only took 42 years.

title: Funk #49

description: Joe Walsh's breakup rocker opens Thirds, the last James Gang studio album with him in the band. It became their highest-charting single and stayed in Walsh's live sets for decades.

pops.text: This is the opening track on Thirds (1971) — and unlike the group-written 'Funk #49,' Walsh wrote this one all by himself.
It's a breakup song with its boots on: 'Seems to me, you just turn your pretty head and walk away' is the whole argument in one line.
Thirds was Walsh's last studio album with the James Gang. He left later in 1971 — yes, he really did walk away.
Check the original LP credits: Walsh is listed for 'guitar, vocals, and train wreck.' That is an official job title now.
The 'train wreck' is the fade-out: multi-tracked lead guitars cascading and clashing on purpose. Headphones recommended for the full pile-up.
Walsh explained the wreck: everything on 10, fuzz all the way up, guitar thrown in the air, put on the ground and jumped on. Pete Townshend-style.
He skipped setting it on fire, joking you can't see that on an album — 'That would have been stupid.' Sound logic.
At No. 51 on the Billboard Hot 100, this was the James Gang's best-placing single — one spot-count ahead of 'Funk #49' at No. 59.
Thirds climbed to No. 27 and went gold in July 1972, after Walsh had already left the band.
Walsh liked it too much to leave it behind: he re-cut it solo in 1976, and the Eagles made it a Walsh spotlight in their live shows.

title: Walk Away

description: Jamiroquai's warning about technology and genetic tinkering, wrapped in acid-jazz funk. Its moving-room video won Video of the Year at the 1997 MTV VMAs and became an era-defining clip.

pops.text: The inspiration was underground — literally: Jay Kay saw Sapporo, Japan's bustling underground city and wrote about a future lived below the surface.
Kay wrote it with keyboardist Toby Smith, the band's musical co-pilot. It's the second single from Travelling Without Moving (1996).
Listen at the very start: a sound sampled from Alien appears — the sequence tied to the Nostromo's S.O.S. signal in the 1979 film.
The floor is NOT moving. Director Jonathan Glazer locked the camera to a wall and moved the whole room on wheels around a plain grey floor.
A real moving floor was priced out at about £280,000 for the rig alone. The finished video cost about £150,000 total — walls were cheaper.
Some sofas were fixed to the walls, so they look frozen while actually moving; others sat loose, so they look like they're gliding by themselves.
Look closely and the illusion wobbles: the moving walls weren't fully rigid and can be seen wiggling slightly in some shots.
Filmed on 12 August 1996 in London, the video earned 10 nominations at the 1997 MTV VMAs and won four, including Video of the Year.
Chart run: No. 1 in Iceland, No. 3 in the UK, and No. 38 on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks when it reached the US in 1997.
It also won Jamiroquai a Grammy for Best Pop Performance by a Duo or Group. The parent album became the best-selling funk album in history.

title: Virtual Insanity

description: The lead single from Synkronized is pure disco-funk joy about dancing your blues away. Five years later, Napoleon Dynamite turned it into one of cinema's most imitated dance scenes.

pops.text: Released 24 May 1999 as the lead single from Synkronized, Jamiroquai's fourth album — and it opens that album, too.
Jay Kay is the sole credited songwriter here. His brief was simple: he has 'canned heat' in his heels and needs to dance the blues away.
Director Jonas Åkerlund shot the video: Kay wakes in his London flat, puts his shoes on, talks to a wall — then phases straight through it.
From there Kay dances on a dining table, swings from a chandelier, floats defying gravity, and ends up back in bed where he started.
Åkerlund came in hot: he'd just made Madonna's 'Ray of Light' video and The Prodigy's notorious 'Smack My Bitch Up.'
The album version runs 5:30; radio got a 3:19 edit. Even Napoleon only needed about half the can.
Chart heat: No. 4 on the UK Singles Chart and Jamiroquai's second No. 1 on the US Dance Club Play chart.
The Napoleon connection started earlier: filming his short Peluca, director Jared Hess had leftover film, a car radio playing this song, and Jon Heder dancing.
For Napoleon Dynamite (2004), Heder freestyled it: he danced to this, a Michael Jackson track and another Jamiroquai song, until he felt ready to puke — his words.
There was no choreography to memorize — Heder has said if you ask him to 'do the dance,' he'd just freestyle again. The song later joined Just Dance 2024.

title: Canned Heat

description: A nostalgic look back at teenage nights at a Seymour, Indiana teen club, from The Lonesome Jubilee. Fiddle and accordion drive a hit that topped Billboard's rock chart and hit No. 8 pop.

pops.text: Billing check: in 1987 he was still John Cougar Mellencamp. This was the second single from his ninth album, The Lonesome Jubilee.
No fireworks involved: the 'Cherry Bomb' was a teenage hangout — the real spot was The Last Exit teen club in a church basement in Seymour, Indiana.
Mellencamp has described those nights as young men and women 'rubbing up against each other, passionately.' Dancing, officially.
That swirling sound is the Jubilee experiment: Lisa Germano's fiddle and John Cascella's accordion front and center in a rock hit.
It wasn't a one-man vocal: several band voices trade lines, a trick Mellencamp credited to Sly and the Family Stone's multi-vocal approach.
Listen for backup singer Crystal Taliefero taking the 'winter days they last forever' line — one of the song's most-remembered moments.
The album was cut at Mellencamp's Belmont Mall Studio in Indiana, with sessions running from September 1986 to June 1987.
The video makes its point quietly: an interracial couple dances intimately by a jukebox — Mellencamp, who'd played in an interracial band, wanted music's mixing on screen.
Double chart-topper energy: No. 8 on the Billboard Hot 100, No. 12 Adult Contemporary — and No. 1 on Billboard's Album Rock Tracks.
The Lonesome Jubilee peaked at No. 6 and spawned four singles. Two years earlier, Mellencamp had co-founded Farm Aid — heartland wasn't just a sound.

title: Cherry Bomb

description: John Cougar's soul-tinged 1981 single from Nothin' Matters and What If It Did — a young man on a date, long on nerves and short on cool lines. It reached No. 17 and became his biggest American hit yet.

pops.text: Name check: in 1981 he was billed as John Cougar. The 'Cougar' was imposed by manager Tony DeFries, who thought Mellencamp sounded too hillbilly to sell.
This comes from his fourth album, Nothin' Matters and What If It Did, released in 1980 — the record that set up his breakthrough.
Producer power: soul pioneer Steve Cropper, of Booker T. & the M.G.'s, produced the album. Mellencamp was aiming for a soul song, and hired accordingly.
Cropper had form: he co-wrote soul classics including 'In the Midnight Hour' and '(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay.' That groove was no accident.
Released as the album's second single on March 14, 1981, following lead single 'This Time,' which had peaked at No. 27.
The story is pure young-date nerves: he portrays a young man out with a woman who is enamored with him, while he admits he knows no good come-ons and no cool lines.
Chart verdict: it climbed to No. 17 on the Billboard Hot 100 — at the time his biggest American hit, passing 'I Need a Lover' and 'This Time.'
The video goes full James Brown: Cougar drops to his knees cradling the mic while his band, dressed like Brown's Famous Flames, tries to drag him away.
Watch the sax solo: nobody on screen is playing it — the pianist simply mouths the notes. An interesting choice, as one writer politely put it.
He later disowned the album, calling the singles 'stupid little pop songs' and saying, 'I take no credit for that record.' It still took 11 years to go Platinum — and paved the way for American Fool.

title: Ain't Even Done With The Night

description: The lead single from Khruangbin's second album Con Todo El Mundo (2018), a wordless groove drawing on pre-revolution Iranian pop and a classic breakbeat. Its video celebrates Iranian women artists before 1979.

pops.text: Wordless wonder: not a single word is spoken on this track. Mark Speer's spindly guitar riff does the job of a chorus all by itself.
Lead single from the trio's second album, Con Todo El Mundo, released January 26, 2018 — and their first album for Dead Oceans. 'Maria También' is track 3, at 3 minutes 10 seconds.
The album title means 'with all the world' and was a tribute to bassist Laura Lee's Mexican-American grandfather. The music takes the title literally.
Band homework: for this record Speer listened to Iranian pop star Googoosh more than anyone else — he calls her 'the Michael Jackson of Iran.'
The band say this was the first song written for the album, arriving after a long dry spell of writer's block. It remains one of their favorites.
What you're hearing, they explain, reflects Middle Eastern music — particularly from pre-revolution Iran — rather than the Thai funk of their debut.
Hip-hop heads, listen for the break: its beat is straight-up 'Apache.' Speer once ran sound at a Houston youth center where breakdancers taught kids to B-boy.
Like their first albums, it was shaped in the band's barn studio in Burton, Texas — Speer's family barn, in a town of about 300 people.
The official video, directed by Chris Boyle from a concept by Sanam Petri and Laura Lee, celebrates Iranian women before the 1979 revolution — their creativity, freedom and expression.
The video features a large network of Iranian artists, singers, dancers and songwriters who have been exiled or silenced since that revolution. A groove with a memorial built in.

title: Maria También

description: A compact, chant-along highlight of Khruangbin's 2015 debut The Universe Smiles Upon You — just 2 minutes 39 seconds of Thai-funk-inspired groove, and among the first Khruangbin tracks to feature vocals.

pops.text: Short and sweet: the studio version runs just 2 minutes 39 seconds. Live, Khruangbin have stretched it past seven minutes.
This is track 6 on the band's debut album, The Universe Smiles Upon You, released November 6, 2015, on Night Time Stories.
Conceived as an instrumental outfit, the band surprised themselves here — this is among the first Khruangbin recordings with vocals, alongside 'White Gloves' and 'Balls and Pins.'
The debut was recorded at their spiritual home: a remote barn deep in the Texas countryside, where their first rehearsals took place.
Road-trip curriculum: on the long drives to that barn, the trio devoured 1960s and '70s Thai cassettes sourced from the cult Monrakplengthai blog.
Those cassettes shaped the scales they used and the inflection of their melodies — Thai funk, filtered through spacious Texas countryside.
Origin story: guitarist Mark Speer and drummer Donald 'DJ' Johnson first played together in a Houston church gospel band, years before Khruangbin existed.
The band's name is Thai for 'airplane' — it was Laura Lee's favorite word while she was learning Thai, picked just before their first gig.
For Record Store Day 2016 it got its own remix 12-inch: an extended version fans had requested, plus a Vuelo dub remix made for a beach-festival sunrise.
Full circle: in 2025 the band surprise-released a re-recorded debut, The Universe Smiles Upon You ii, tracked in that same barn — with a kinetic, extended 'People Everywhere' aboard.

title: People Everywhere (Still Alive)

description: Kings of Leon's breakthrough 2008 lead single from Only by the Night — a misheard studio joke that became their first No. 1 in the UK, Ireland, Australia and Finland, and won them their first Grammy.

pops.text: Accidental title: the song began as 'Set Us on Fire.' A sound mixer walked in, misheard it as 'Sex on fire, huh?' — the joke stuck, and so did the title.
Caleb Followill admits the lyric arrived almost by accident: messing with the melody, he sang 'this sex is on fire' before he really knew what he was saying.
Lead single from the band's fourth album, Only by the Night, released in August 2008, and written by all four Followills — three brothers and their cousin.
It was produced by the band's longtime collaborators Angelo Petraglia and Jacquire King, the team behind the whole Only by the Night album.
Breakthrough: this gave Kings of Leon their first No. 1 single in Australia, Finland, Ireland and the United Kingdom.
In the UK it hit No. 1 on digital downloads alone, before its physical release — a still-new trick for a rock single in 2008.
By September 2009 it was Britain's second most-downloaded digital single ever, and it had sold 1.2 million copies in the UK by November 2012.
America caught up more slowly: No. 1 on the Hot Modern Rock Tracks chart, but No. 56 on the Billboard Hot 100.
The video was directed by Sophie Muller. The band have said they were dissatisfied with how they were portrayed in it — all that smoldering took some getting used to.
It won the band their first Grammy, Best Rock Vocal Performance by a Duo or Group, in 2009 — and topped Triple J's Hottest 100 in Australia for 2008.

title: Sex on Fire

description: The second single from Only by the Night (2008) — Caleb Followill's on-the-road apology to his bandmates, turned into a No. 4 US hit that won three Grammys, including Record of the Year.

pops.text: Sorry, in song form: Caleb Followill wrote this as an apology to his bandmates after a drunken fight on tour — an olive branch with a stadium chorus.
The fallout happened around a Glasgow date in December 2007. Caleb has said the tune came to him at soundcheck the next day, when nobody was making eye contact.
Songfacts traces the melody to an unlikely source: Caleb speeding up 'Up Where We Belong,' the Joe Cocker and Jennifer Warnes theme from An Officer and a Gentleman.
He told Mojo the melody and the line 'I could use somebody, somebody like you' came on the road; at home he finished what he called one of his most heartfelt lyrics ever.
Second single from Only by the Night, released December 8, 2008. Its performance video was directed by Sophie Muller, who also directed 'Sex on Fire.'
Slow-burn smash: it reached No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 in September 2009 — the band's first US Top 10 hit — and spent 57 weeks on that chart.
Radio sweep: it became only the fourth song in history to top the Mainstream Top 40, Adult Top 40, Alternative and Triple A charts all at once.
In Australia it sat at No. 1 on the Official Airplay Chart for six consecutive weeks. In the UK it peaked at No. 2 and lingered for 77 weeks in the Top 75.
Recording quirk: for Only by the Night, producer Jacquire King recorded Caleb's vocals in a sound-lock chamber between the control room and live room at Nashville's Blackbird Studio D.
At the 2010 Grammys it won three awards — Record of the Year, Best Rock Song and Best Rock Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocal — and was also nominated for Song of the Year.

title: Use Somebody
